chapter.name: Amendment of the Constitution

concepts.name: Article 368: nature of the power and the stages of the procedure
concepts.description: The source of the amending power in Part XX, the limit set by the basic structure, and the stages from introduction of the bill to Presidential assent.
concepts.idea: Article 368 lets Parliament amend the Constitution by an eight-stage procedure: a bill in either House, special majority in each House separately, ratification by half the states for federal provisions, and obligatory assent.
concepts.rule: Article 368 in Part XX deals with the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure, and Parliament acts in exercise of its constituent power by addition, variation or repeal; it cannot amend the basic structure, as ruled in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The procedure is neither as easy as Britain's nor as difficult as the USA's, so the Constitution is a synthesis of flexible and rigid. An amendment bill can be introduced only in either House of Parliament, not in the state legislatures, by a minister or a private member and without the President's prior permission. It must be passed in each House separately by a special majority, a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting, with no provision for a joint sitting on disagreement. A bill amending federal provisions must also be ratified by the legislatures of half the states by a simple majority. The President must then give assent, neither withholding it nor returning the bill, as the 24th Amendment Act of 1971 made obligatory, and the Constitution stands amended according to the Act.
concepts.example: A bill to change the lists of the Seventh Schedule is passed by a special majority in each House, ratified by half of the state legislatures, and then receives the President's obligatory assent.

questions.q: The power of Parliament to amend the Constitution, and the procedure for doing so, are dealt with in one Article placed in Part XX of the Constitution. Which one of the following is that Article?
questions.e: Article 368 in Part XX deals with the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure.
w: Article 13 is the Article whose word 'law' was at issue in the amendment cases; it does not lay down the amending procedure.
Article 279-A is the Article to which the GST Council provision is relatedfootnote 3).
Article 32 deals with remedies for enforcement of Fundamental Rightsfootnote 6).

questions.q: A Constitution Amendment Bill has been passed by both Houses of Parliament (and ratified by the states, where necessary) and is presented to the President. Which one of the following is the position of the President?
questions.a: He must assent; he can neither withhold assent nor return the bill
o: He must assent; he can neither withhold assent nor return the bill
He may withhold assent, but he cannot return the bill
He may return the bill once, but must assent when it is passed again
He may withhold assent until half of the state legislatures have ratified it
questions.e: The President must give his assent; he can neither withhold assent nor return the bill, as the 24th Amendment Act of 1971 made assent obligatory.
w: Withholding assent is not open to him; assent is obligatory.
He cannot return the bill for reconsideration at all, because the 24th Amendment made assent obligatory.
Ratification, where required, comes before the bill is presented to him, and his assent is obligatory in any case.

questions.q: In which one of the following cases did the Supreme Court rule that Parliament, in exercising its constituent power under Article 368, cannot amend the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
questions.e: The bar on amending the basic structure was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The earlier cases went the other way: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) allowed amendment of Fundamental Rights, and Golak Nath (1967) denied it altogether.
w: Golak Nath held Fundamental Rights to be 'transcendental and immutable' and was overruled in 1973.
Shankari Prasad held that Parliament's power under Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Sajjan Singh re-affirmed the Shankari Prasad stand.

questions.q: A Constitution Amendment Bill is passed by one House of Parliament by the required majority, but the other House does not agree to it. Which one of the following is the position under Article 368?
questions.a: No provision exists for a joint sitting to deliberate on and pass the bill
o: No provision exists for a joint sitting to deliberate on and pass the bill
The President may summon a joint sitting, where a simple majority decides the bill
A joint sitting decides the bill by the same special majority
The bill is held over six months and then passed on the vote of the Lok Sabha alone
questions.e: Under Article 368 each House must pass the Constitution Amendment Bill separately by the required majority; in case of disagreement there is no provision for a joint sitting. An ordinary bill, by contrast, can be resolved at a joint sitting under Article 108.
w: No joint sitting exists for this purpose; a simple-majority joint sitting under Article 108 applies only to ordinary bills.
Even with a special majority, a joint sitting is not available for a Constitution Amendment Bill.
Article 368 has no waiting period or Lok Sabha override; each House must pass the bill separately.

concepts.name: Constituent power compared with the ordinary legislative process
concepts.description: Where the constituent power lies, how amending a Constitution resembles and differs from making an ordinary law, and the cases on whether an amendment is a 'law' under Article 13.
concepts.idea: The constituent power rests in Parliament and only in few cases the states, its process resembles ordinary legislation except for the special majority and no joint sitting, and the courts have debated whether an amendment is a 'law' under Article 13.
concepts.rule: India has no special body such as a Constitutional Convention or Constitutional Assembly for amendment; the constituent power is vested in Parliament and in few cases in the state legislatures, which, can initiate nothing except a resolution asking Parliament to create or abolish a legislative council. Apart from the special majority, amendment bills are passed like ordinary bills, but a joint sitting is available for an ordinary bill and not for an amendment bill. Some matters are changed by a simple majority outside Article 368 and are not deemed amendments for its purposes. In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964) the Supreme Court held that 'law' in Article 13 means only ordinary law and not constituent law, so Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights; Golak Nath (1967) reversed this, holding Fundamental Rights 'transcendental and immutable'. Parliament's 24th Amendment (1971) amended Articles 13 and 368 to restore its power, and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and upheld that Act.
concepts.example: A resolution of a state legislature asking Parliament to abolish its legislative council is the only proposal a state legislature can send, and Parliament may approve it, reject it or do nothing.

questions.q: Critics note that India has no special body, such as a Constitutional Convention or a Constitutional Assembly, for amending the Constitution. In whom does the constituent power then lie?
questions.a: In Parliament, and only in a few cases also in the state legislatures
o: In Parliament, and only in a few cases also in the state legislatures
In a Constitutional Convention called by Parliament when needed
In the state legislatures, with Parliament giving only its approval
In a Constitutional Assembly elected afresh for each amendment
questions.e: The constituent power is vested in Parliament and only in few cases in the state legislatures; there is no special body for amendment.
w: No Constitutional Convention or Assembly is provided for in the Constitution; the power lies with Parliament.
It is the other way round: Parliament holds the power and the states join in only a few cases.
No such Assembly is provided for amendments.

questions.q: Some provisions of the Constitution can be changed by a simple majority of Parliament, as in an ordinary law. How are such changes treated for the purposes of Article 368?

o: They are not deemed to be amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368
They are amendments under Article 368 that need no ratification by the states
They are amendments under Article 368 only if they touch the Fundamental Rights
They are amendments under Article 368 only when passed by a majority of the total membership
questions.e: These amendments are notably not deemed to be amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
w: They are outside the scope of Article 368 altogether.
The Fundamental Rights are amended by special majority under Article 368, not by this route.
A majority of the total membership is part of the special majority, which this route does not need.

questions.q: In the Shankari Prasad case (1951), the Supreme Court held that the word 'law' in Article 13 should be understood to cover which of the following?

questions.e: The word 'law' in Article 13 includes only ordinary laws and not the constitutional amendment acts (constituent laws).
w: That is the view the court took later in Golak Nath, reversing Shankari Prasad.
The court drew its line between ordinary laws and constituent laws, not between Parliament and the states.
The case concerned the First Amendment Act (1951), a law made after the Constitution came into force.

questions.q: Which one of the following amendment acts declared that there is no limitation on the constituent power of Parliament and that no amendment can be questioned in any court?

w: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368 after Golak Nath, but did not bar all court challenges.

w: Article 31 was not amended by the 24th Amendment Act; it amended Articles 13 and 368.

concepts.name: Three ways of amending the Constitution
concepts.description: Amendment by simple majority outside Article 368, by special majority, and by special majority with the consent of half the states, and the provisions that fall in each.
concepts.idea: Provisions of the Constitution are amended in three ways, and which way applies depends on whether the matter is ordinary, general or federal.
concepts.rule: Article 368 provides two types of amendment, special majority and special majority with ratification by half the states, while other articles allow amendment by a simple majority of Parliament, which is not deemed an amendment for Article 368; hence the Constitution can be amended in three ways. The simple-majority matters include new states and boundaries, legislative councils, the Second Schedule, quorum, MPs' salaries, citizenship, elections, delimitation, Union territories and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules. Most provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, need a special majority, where 'total membership' means the House as constituted, irrespective of vacancies or absentees. Federal provisions, such as the election of the President, the executive power of the Union and the states, the Supreme Court and high courts, legislative distribution, the GST Council added by the 101st Amendment (2016), the Seventh Schedule lists, representation of states and Article 368 itself, also need consent of half the state legislatures by simple majority, with no time limit and no effect from the inaction of the rest.
concepts.example: Fixing the quorum in Parliament needs only a simple majority, a change to Fundamental Rights needs a special majority, and a change to the lists of the Seventh Schedule also needs the consent of half the states.

concepts.name: Criticism and evaluation of the amendment procedure
concepts.description: The seven grounds of criticism, the defence of the procedure, and the remarks of Nehru, Ambedkar and Wheare.
concepts.idea: Critics fault the procedure for vesting everything in Parliament, leaving gaps on the states and the Houses, but it is judged a good balance between flexibility and rigidity.
concepts.rule: Critics point out that there is no special amending body, that state legislatures cannot initiate amendments except the council resolution, that most of the Constitution can be amended by Parliament alone and that only half of the states (three-fourths in the USA) are needed in few cases. They add that no time frame is set for state ratification and the Constitution is silent on withdrawal of approval, that there is no joint sitting for a deadlock unlike for an ordinary bill, that the process resembles ordinary legislation, and that the sketchy provisions invite litigation. Despite these defects the procedure is regarded as simple, successful and neither so flexible as to allow whims nor so rigid as to be incapable of adapting, a balance Wheare endorsed. Nehru said there is no permanence in a Constitution; Ambedkar said the Assembly provided a facile procedure unlike Canada, America or Australia; Wheare called the variety wise but rare.
concepts.example: Nehru warned that a rigid and permanent Constitution would stop the growth of a living people, a view cited in favour of a flexible procedure.

questions.q: Critics of the Indian amending procedure contrast it with the United States on the share of states whose consent is needed. What is the corresponding requirement for ratifying an amendment in the USA?

concepts.name: Judicial limits on the amending power: the basic structure doctrine
concepts.description: The cycle of judgements and amendments from Kesavananda Bharati to Waman Rao, the present position, and the elements of the basic structure.
concepts.idea: The Supreme Court bars Parliament from altering the basic structure, and Parliament's efforts to remove this limit were struck down.
concepts.rule: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and upheld the 24th Amendment, allowing Parliament to abridge Fundamental Rights, but laid down that its constituent power under Article 368 cannot alter the basic structure. Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) applied the doctrine to invalidate a 39th Amendment provision keeping election disputes of the Prime Minister and Speaker out of the courts. The 42nd Amendment (1976) declared no limit on the constituent power and barred any court challenge; Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated this as it excluded judicial review, a basic feature, and held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature. Waman Rao (1980) applied the doctrine to amendments after April 24, 1973. Today Parliament may amend any part including Fundamental Rights without affecting the basic structure, which the Supreme Court is yet to define, though about twenty elements have emerged and the table of basic-structure elements maps them to cases.
concepts.example: A law that removes the courts' power to review a constitutional amendment would be struck down because judicial review is a basic feature, as in Minerva Mills.

questions.q: In the Waman Rao case (1980), the Supreme Court clarified that the doctrine of the basic structure applies to constitutional amendments enacted after which of the following?
o: The date of the Golak Nath judgement
The date of the 42nd Amendment Act (1976)
questions.e: Waman Rao clarified that the doctrine would apply to amendments enacted after April 24, 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgement.
w: Golak Nath (1967) took the opposite view of the amending power and is not the cut-off the court fixed.
The cut-off is earlier than 1976; the 42nd Amendment itself was a reaction to the doctrine.
The doctrine did not date from the commencement of the Constitution; it was laid down in 1973.

questions.a: Powers of the Supreme Court under Article 32

questions.e: Ram Jethmalani (2011) is linked to the powers of the Supreme Court under Article 32.
w: These are the elements associated with L. Chandra Kumar (1997) and Madras Bar Association (2014).
Effective access to justice was declared in the Central Coal Fields case (1980).
Independence of the judiciary was declared in the Kumar Padma Prasad case (1992).

questions.q: In Minerva Mills (1980) the Supreme Court invalidated the 42nd Amendment's provision that no amendment could be questioned in any court. What reason did it give?
questions.a: The provision excluded judicial review, which is a basic feature of the Constitution
o: The provision excluded judicial review, which is a basic feature of the Constitution
The provision had been enacted without ratification by half of the state legislatures
The provision sought to transfer the amending power from Parliament to the states
The provision applied to amendments enacted before April 24, 1973
questions.e: Minerva Mills invalidated the provision as it excluded judicial review, which is a basic feature of the Constitution.
w: The 42nd Amendment's clause did not fail for want of ratification; the Court's reason was that it excluded judicial review, a basic feature.
The provision declared Parliament's constituent power unlimited; it did not move it to the states.
The date of April 24, 1973 was fixed in Waman Rao as the point from which the doctrine applies, and the 42nd Amendment came after it.

questions.q: What is the present position on the amending power of Parliament under Article 368?
questions.a: Parliament may amend any part, including Fundamental Rights, but not the basic structure
o: Parliament may amend any part, including Fundamental Rights, but not the basic structure
Parliament may amend any part, including the basic structure, but not Fundamental Rights
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights only with the consent of half of the state legislatures
Parliament may amend only those parts that do not include Fundamental Rights or Directive Principles
questions.e: Parliament under Article 368 can amend any part of the Constitution including the Fundamental Rights but without affecting the basic structure.
w: This reverses the position: the basic structure is the limit, not the Fundamental Rights.
No such ratification condition applies; Fundamental Rights are amendable by a special majority of Parliament, subject to the basic structure.
Fundamental Rights can be amended, provided the basic structure is not affected.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT an element of the basic structure recognised in the judgements of the Supreme Court?

questions.e: The right to property is not an element of the basic structure (it ceased to be a Fundamental Right by the 44th Amendment). Effective access to justice, free and fair elections, and harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles have all been recognised in judgements.
w: Effective access to justice was recognised as a basic feature in the Central Coal Fields case (1980).
Free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature, for example in the Indira Nehru Gandhi case (1975).
Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was recognised in the Minerva Mills case (1980).

Statement 2 is incorrect: Golak Nath reversed that stand and held that an amendment is a 'law' under Article 13. Statement 3 is correct: the provision affected the basic structure and was beyond the amending power. Statement 4 is incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the validity of the 24th Amendment Act while laying down the basic structure doctrine. So only two statements are correct.
w: 'None' miscounts: statements 1 and 3 are correct.
'Only one' miscounts: statements 1 and 3 are both correct.
'Only three' miscounts: statements 2 and 4 are incorrect.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The Supreme Court in the Indira Nehru Gandhi case (1975) invalidated a provision of the 39th Amendment Act.
Statement-II: That provision kept election disputes involving the Prime Minister and the Speaker outside the jurisdiction of all courts, and so affected the basic structure.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) the Supreme Court invalidated clause (4) of Article 329-A inserted by the 39th Amendment Act. Statement-II is correct: that provision kept election disputes involving the Prime Minister and the Speaker outside the jurisdiction of all courts. The Court held it beyond the amending power because it affected the basic structure, which is the ground for Statement-I.
w: 'Both correct without II explaining' is rejected: Statement-II does explain Statement-I, as the Court held the provision beyond the amending power because it affected the basic structure.
'I correct and II incorrect' is rejected: Statement-II is correct, since the provision removed election disputes of the Prime Minister and Speaker from all courts.
'I incorrect and II correct' is rejected: Statement-I is correct, since the Court invalidated the provision in 1975.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The Supreme Court has so far fully defined what constitutes the basic structure of the Constitution.
Statement-II: Various judgements have produced a list of features treated as elements of the basic structure.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
o: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
questions.e: Statement-I is incorrect: the Supreme Court has not exhaustively defined the basic structure; the doctrine has developed case by case. Statement-II is correct: judgements have produced a list of features such as judicial review, federalism and secularism that are treated as elements of the basic structure.
w: 'Both correct with II explaining' is rejected: Statement-I is incorrect, since the Supreme Court has not fully defined the basic structure.
'Both correct without II explaining' is rejected: Statement-I is incorrect, since the Supreme Court has not fully defined the basic structure.
'I correct and II incorrect' is rejected: Statement-I is incorrect, since the Supreme Court has not fully defined the basic structure; Statement-II is correct, since judgements have listed elements.
